title: The Online Cancer Nutrition Misinformation: A framework of behavior change based on exposure to cancer nutrition misinformation
screen_reason: Content analysis of 103 Pinterest pins retrieved with 'cancer recipe' and 'recipe for cancer'. The coding is a claim-type inventory rather than a truth verdict: no pin was ever rated true or false, and the authors say outright that 'clearly defining nutrition misinformation online remains challenging'. One coded category nonetheless entails falsity on its face — pins purporting that food or diet CURES cancer (10.7%) — and coding the presence of a claim that is false by scientific consensus is functionally a falsity classification with the ground truth built into the code definition. I take that one row as CONTENT and flag it borderline. JUDGEMENT CALL FOR THE ADJUDICATOR: an adjudicator applying §3 strictly ('CONTENT only if items are judged for truth/falsity against an external ground truth') could reasonably screen this paper OUT as a claim-inventory with no veracity coding. The prevention (41.8%) and treatment (27.2%) claim categories are deliberately NOT rows, because diet genuinely does affect cancer risk and prognosis — the paper says so itself — and those claims can therefore be true.

estimates.country: Not stated; English-language Pinterest search (authors US-based; the paper notes Pinterest is widely used in the United States)
estimates.date: June 2020, sampled at 3 time points a day for 2 weeks
estimates.measure_type: % of cancer-recipe Pinterest pins whose content purported that food or diet CURES cancer
estimates.value_raw: 10.7% of 103 pins (11 pins) purported to cure cancer; prevent 41.8%, treat 27.2%
estimates.denominator: 103 unique Pinterest pins (post plus linked landing page) returned by the searches 'cancer recipe' and 'recipe for cancer', after duplicates were removed
estimates.definition: A pin counted in the numerator if the pin or its linked landing page made a claim that a food, diet or nutrition practice cures cancer. Coding recorded whether the claim was present, not whether it was independently verified; the category is nonetheless false by scientific consensus. Related coding in the same sample: 11 pins (10.7%) directly claimed food- or diet-based therapies were a viable, or in some cases preferable, alternative to conventional treatment.
estimates.misinfo_def: No operational definition; the paper defines the neighbouring concept of food faddism as "the exaggerated belief that certain foods or food components can cure or cause disease or have special health benefits" and concedes that "clearly defining nutrition misinformation online remains challenging"
estimates.source_quote: common, with content that purported to prevent (41.8%), treat (27.2%), or cure (10.7%) cancer.
estimates.page_loc: p. 2540 Abstract, Results sentence; same figures in Results, 'Nutrition-Related Claims in Cancer Nutrition Pins' (p. 2542) and Figure 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Codebook modelled on prior Pinterest studies of vaccination, cannabis and homemade sunscreen, refined over two calibration cycles: 10% of posts inductively coded by two authors, a further 10% double coded by two authors (E.L.W. and M.R.-R.), discrepancies discussed by the research team. Final-round agreement was 86% with Cohen's kappa 0.74, after which the codebook was applied to all pins. No external fact-check or clinical guideline was used as the reference standard.
estimates.moderator_quote: at 3 times daily for 2 weeks. Duplicates were removed for a final sample of n = 103 pins.
estimates.notes: borderline=true and confidence=medium because the paper never classified a pin as false; it classified what claim the pin made. I treat the cure category as a falsity classification because presence of the claim entails falsity, the same way 'X% of videos claimed vaccines cause autism' would. denom_selection=curated: pins were drawn from the ranked search-result feed with a random number generator over positions 1-100, which is a rank-truncated set even though the draw within it was randomised. Single-topic keyword corpus, so denom_scope=topical. platform_norm=other because Pinterest is not in the controlled vocabulary. The 10.7% cure figure and the separately reported 'Eleven pins (10.7%)' claiming diet is a viable alternative to conventional treatment are numerically identical and may or may not be the same 11 pins; the paper does not say, so I did not treat them as two estimates. Note the unit is the pin plus its linked landing page, not the Pinterest post alone.

missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately not extracted, and the reason matters: (1) prevention claims (41.8%) and treatment claims (27.2%) — a claim that diet reduces cancer risk or helps during treatment can be true, and the paper's own introduction says a healthy diet may reduce primary cancer risk and improve prognosis, so these categories do not identify false content; (2) 'Approximately 40% made claims using anticancer buzz words' — vague marketing language, not a falsifiable claim, and the figure is approximate rather than exact; (3) the claim-category shares (at least one cancer-related health concern claim 59/103 = 57.3%, food or food components 85/103 = 82.5%, general health food 56/103 = 54.4%, no cancer- or health-related claim 5%) — topic inventories with no veracity judgement; (4) the 11 pins (10.7%) claiming diet is a viable or preferable alternative to conventional treatment — numerically identical to the cure figure and possibly the same pins, so recording both would risk double counting the same 11 items; (5) conspiracy claims 'were rare (2 occasions)' — a bare count without a stated share, and 2/103 would be my own computation, though it is exact; an adjudicator wanting a very strict misinformation row could use it; (6) validity-indicator shares (personal anecdotes 21.6%, academic/government citations 28.2%, disclaimers 36%) and all of Table 2's claim-by-indicator cross-tabs — presentation features, not falsity; (7) all descriptive pin/creator characteristics (for-profit 68%, selling a product 48.5%, no health credentials 77.7%, individual posters 67%); (8) 'a 95% chance of reaching content making a health claim' and 'an approximate 1 in 3 chance of linking to a page selling a product' in the Discussion are rhetorical restatements of the 5%-no-claim and 34% figures, not new estimates; (9) mean claims per pin 6.03 (SD 3.94) is a mean, not a share.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of Pinterest. In June 2020 the searches 'cancer recipe' and 'recipe for cancer' were run at 3 time points a day for 2 weeks; at each point a random number generator over positions 1-100 selected 5 applicable posts, which were screenshotted and their links stored; duplicates removed for a final sample of 103 pins, each pin comprising the post and its linked landing page. No response rate applies. 58 variables coded per pin, covering descriptives, cancer claims and nutrition claims, plus validity indicators (academic or government citations, personal anecdotes, disclaimers). Reliability: two inductive/double-coding cycles on 10% of posts each, research-team adjudication, final agreement 86% with kappa 0.74 before full application. Main weakness for this review: no variable records whether a claim was true, and the authors explicitly decline to define misinformation operationally, so all 'misinformation' language in the paper rests on the framing rather than on a measurement.
